title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N=500 deterministic intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN, ACL, and static-route clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal (gpt-5-mini) and (2) guarded — the same LLM proposal screened by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); paired contingency: n11=499, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10000, seed = 1729). Model-call accounting recorded 501 model calls and a single repair-stage call. On this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the marginal numeric verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small but a single archived discordant episode shows the loop corrected at least one real baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle and are available for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being adopted for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, change planning, limited automated repair). System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A common mitigation pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks properties, and repair/regeneration is applied when violations are found. Despite broad interest, controlled measurements that isolate the verifier’s marginal contribution under reproducible conditions are scarce. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to address a focused operational question: how much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a G→V→R loop reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals compared to LLM-only proposals, when tasks and topologies are canonical and restricted to verifier-modeled features? We report the preregistered design, artifact-backed execution accounting, confirmatory analysis, and interpretation boundaries.
sections.related_work: Deterministic and formal network-verification techniques (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers and related tooling) can check reachability, isolation, and update-safety from configuration artifacts [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems integrate LLMs into intent-driven pipelines and consistently advocate validators and guardrails for safe automation [Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair and verifier-assisted self-correction have been proposed or instantiated across structured-generation domains; however, published controlled ablations that quantify verifier effect size specifically for LLM-driven NetOps pipelines remain limited [INTA, 2025; Confucius, 2025]. Failure-mode studies documenting hallucination, overconfidence, and tool failures further motivate guarded pipelines [Owen, 2026]. Our experimental contribution is an artifact-backed, preregistered, paired measurement that isolates verifier+repair impact under constrained, reproducible semantics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and study scope: The study was preregistered prior to execution (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026). Research question: Does a verifier+single-repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations relative to the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback, under shared-initial-candidate semantics? Confirmatory hypothesis: guarded produces a lower violation rate than baseline (paired within-task). The design, inclusion/exclusion rules, estimands, analysis executor, and multiplicity plan were frozen in the preregistration. Task generation and strata: 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks were created by a seeded generator and stratified as preregistered into three canonical clusters: VLAN-change = 167, ACL-change = 167, static-route-change = 166. Only features modeled by the deterministic validator were included; tasks referencing unmodeled features were routed to an unmodeled cohort and excluded from the primary analysis (no such exclusions occurred in this run). Generation semantics and orchestration: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' with independent_condition_generation = false: for each task the pipeline produced one shared LLM proposal (the shared initial candidate) which served as the baseline output and was also evaluated by the guarded arm; a guarded repair-stage call was issued only when the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation for that shared candidate. This choice isolates verifier+repair impact conditional on identical initial proposals rather than measuring verifier-guided regeneration. Models, validator, and configuration: LLM = gpt-5-mini (requested model) called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and provider 'openai_responses'; the deterministic validator used in scoring and repair gating was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Model configuration included a max token output budget and single-attempt generation semantics as encoded in the archived model-configuration artifact. Primary estimand and analysis: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. Primary test: exact McNemar two-sided implemented as an exact binomial test on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01), two-sided alpha = 0.05. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with B = 10000 resamples and seed = 1729; resampling unit = task/pair, preserving condition pairing. Missingness and retries: deterministic automated retry policy for transient provider failures was preregistered; missing pairs would be handled per the preregistered plan (primary: drop incomplete pairs; sensitivity: treat missing guarded as failure). Stopping rule: run until the preregistered 500 confirmatory pairs completed or until adapter model-call budget exhausted; the run completed under the adapter limit.
sections.results: Execution accounting and artifact summary: completed pairs = 500; total model calls recorded = 501 reflecting 500 shared initial generations plus 1 repair-stage provider call. Provider-stage accounting recorded shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 1. Primary confirmatory outcomes: baseline_success_count = 499 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998), guarded_success_count = 500 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired 2×2 contingency table (guarded × baseline) is: n11 (both pass) = 499; n10 (guarded pass only) = 1; n01 (baseline pass only) = 0; n00 (both fail) = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention implemented by the analysis executor; paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10000, seed = 1729). Why p = 1.00: the archiving analysis executor implements the exact McNemar two-sided test as an exact two-sided binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01); with n = 1 and the observed discordance concentrated in a single cell (n10 = 1, n01 = 0), the archived exact two-sided convention yields p = 1.00. The archive records both the implementation choice and the numeric result. Repair activity and discordant-pair provenance: observed repair-stage provider calls = 1 across the run; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (guarded corrected a baseline-detected violation). The complete per-task raw records (shared candidate, baseline and guarded scoring outcomes, validator diagnostics, repair prompt/response, and provider-call traces) are archived in the evidence bundle in execution/raw_results.jsonl. The single discordant episode can be located deterministically by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair_ids where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass==0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass==1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this filter returns that episode and its repair-stage provider-call trace. Representative per-task exemplar files and provider-call traces are archived alongside the full raw-results file for independent inspection. Secondary analyses: per-violation-class statistics were not informative because observed violation counts were nearly zero; exploratory subgroup summaries are recorded in the archived analysis artifacts but did not produce additional discordant events.
sections.discussion: The measured effect is constrained by a ceiling effect: the tested model and canonical, verifier-scoped synthetic corpus produced near-perfect initial proposals (499/500 baseline passes), leaving limited room for the verifier+repair loop to improve the pass-rate metric. The observed single corrected episode demonstrates that verifier+repair can amend at least some rare baseline failures, but the measured absolute effect (0.002) is small in this specific regime. Operational implications: (1) When baseline proposal error prevalence is already extremely low, the marginal pass-rate gains from a verifier on this metric may be negligible, though other benefits (audit logs, rollback gating, human triage signals) remain valuable. (2) In production-distribution workloads with higher baseline error rates, broader verifier modeling coverage, or cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, verifier+repair gains measured on safety metrics could be substantially larger. (3) The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate verifier+repair conditional on identical proposals; alternative semantics (verifier-guided regeneration, iterative multi-repair budgets, or independent-condition generation) address different operational questions and may yield different effect sizes. Limitations of inference: (a) the pass/fail composite depends on the verifier’s modeled property set and internal severity mapping; (b) the synthetic corpus covers a restricted set of fields (intent payloads had allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}); (c) only one model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and one validator were tested; (d) repair budget limited to one automated iteration as preregistered. These constraints imply caution when generalizing to heterogeneous, real-world device fleets and intents. Practical recommendation: measure baseline proposal error prevalence and verifier coverage on realistic workloads to prioritize guardrail investment; use G→V→R designs but choose generation semantics and repair budgets appropriate to the operational risk profile.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N=500) that compared an LLM-only pipeline to the same LLM plus a deterministic verifier with up to one automated repair iteration under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Both arms achieved near-perfect verifier pass rates (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the archived two-sided convention). The result quantifies a ceiling-effect regime: an already-accurate LLM leaves limited measured marginal utility for a verifier on the pass-rate metric in this constrained setting. It does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in broader, noisier, or cross-vendor production deployments. All preregistration, execution, prompt, output, validator, provider-call, and analysis artifacts are archived for deterministic re-inspection in the evidence bundle; the single discordant episode and its repair-stage traces are available in execution/raw_results.jsonl for qualitative failure-mode inspection.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; the task payloads in the archive show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 must be interpreted in that context and reflects the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair_id entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass==0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass==1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
